name: Triphala (Ayurvedic three-fruit formula)
short: By mouth with guggul: rash in 2 of 46. Mouth-rinse trials: no side effects reported. Other trials: no serious adverse effects. Raised two drugs' levels in rats; no human interaction data.
text: Triphala is an Ayurvedic combination of three medicinal plants, named in one trial abstract as Terminalia chebula, Terminalia belerica and Phyllanthus emblica. As a mouth rinse (the route closest to the periodontitis page): in a double-blind randomized multicentre trial in 120 hospitalized patients with periodontal diseases, equally divided into three groups (so about 40 used triphala), the authors describe triphala mouthwash as well tolerable with no reported side effects, and in a double-blind randomized trial in 60 female undergraduates (20 per group, one of three groups on triphala), no side effects were reported with the triphala rinse; neither abstract says how side effects were recorded. The abstract of the page's full-mouth disinfection trial does not report adverse events. Other routes and uses: in an open-label, single-arm phase I study in 20 healthy volunteers given an aqueous extract by mouth for four weeks, with physical examinations, blood counts and blood chemistry checked weekly, there were no serious adverse effects, and the volunteers' blood sugar was reduced on days 14 and 35; a 2021 systematic review of 12 randomized trials of triphala for blood lipids, blood sugar and body measures (749 patients; the abstract does not give the route) found that no serious adverse event associated with triphala was reported, and that triphala significantly lowered fasting blood glucose in people with diabetes but not in people without diabetes. In a placebo-controlled trial of triphala combined with guggul (Commiphora mukul) in 90 adults with high cholesterol, 2 of the 46 given the combination (4.3%) developed a hypersensitivity rash, against none on placebo; the trial cannot show which herb was responsible. PubMed searches found no report of liver injury from triphala. Interactions (laboratory and animal data only): in human liver microsomes, triphala extract inhibited the drug-metabolising enzymes CYP1A2, CYP3A4, CYP2C9 and CYP2D6, and in rats given it by mouth it increased the bioavailability of phenacetin and midazolam by about 61% and 41%, while it did not affect the drug transporter P-glycoprotein in a cell model; another laboratory study found that a triphala formulation inhibited CYP3A4 and CYP2D6, less strongly than the positive control; and in rats triphala given with the cancer drug cisplatin slightly raised blood cisplatin levels, which the authors attribute to inhibition of CYP2E1; no human interaction data were found.
